hints: Look first at the cartilage clue in slide 1. Remember how cartilage changes shape as you move down: regular C-rings, then irregular plates, then none at all.
Compare goblet cells and smooth muscle across slides 2 and 3. Think about which airway needs the thickest muscle for its size and which end has the most mucus-secreting cells.
walkthrough:
**Sort out the cartilage rule**

Think of travelling down the airways. The trachea is held open by regular C-shaped rings of cartilage. The bronchus has irregular plates or chunks of cartilage. The bronchiole has no cartilage at all.

Slide 1 has an irregular arrangement of cartilage, so it cannot be trachea or bronchiole. It must be bronchus.

**Use smooth muscle and goblet cells to spot the bronchiole**

As airways get smaller, cartilage and goblet cells decrease, but smooth muscle becomes relatively thicker to control airflow by constriction.

Slide 2 has very few goblet cells plus a thick layer of smooth muscle relative to wall thickness. That is the classic bronchiole pattern.

**Confirm slide 3 as trachea**

The trachea is the widest airway with lots of mucus production to trap dust, so it has many goblet cells, plus supporting blood vessels and smooth muscle tissue (trachealis muscle) between the cartilage ends.

Slide 3 matches this, so slide 1 = bronchus, slide 2 = bronchiole, slide 3 = trachea, which is row A.

options.A: Correct. Slide 1 with irregular cartilage is bronchus, slide 2 with thick relative muscle and few goblets is bronchiole, slide 3 with many goblets is trachea.
options.B: Incorrect. Slide 2 cannot be trachea because trachea has many goblet cells and regular cartilage, not very few goblets with thick relative muscle.
options.C: Incorrect. Slide 1 cannot be trachea because trachea has regular C-shaped cartilage, not an irregular arrangement.
options.D: Incorrect. Slide 1 is not trachea and slide 3 is not bronchiole, since bronchioles lack cartilage and have very few goblet cells, not many.
